title: Non-blocking follow-ups from backend-profit-target-weekly-channel-followups PR #223 review
description: Non-blocking findings from pr-reviewer's full review of PR #223 (backend-profit-target-weekly-channel-followups, the check_profit_target_wording.py guard script), recorded here per CLAUDE.md's convention so they aren't lost once the PR merges. All six were verified as real, demonstrated gaps in the guard's own robustness (confirmed by directly constructing inputs and running the affected functions), not currently-live false positives/negatives against the real repo tree -- and critically, none of them defeat the guard's actual protection for the 8 known regression-prone files: the per-file positive check (check_known_files_mention_weekly) operates on whole-file text at the character-window level, not per physical line, so it independently still catches a reversion in any of those 8 files even where the repo-wide negative check's line-based scanning is fooled (verified directly by reverting schemas.py's `source` field to the old stale wording, wrapped across lines matching the file's own dominant style for long Field descriptions elsewhere -- the negative check missed it, the positive check still caught it). That's why these are follow-ups rather than blocking findings.

checklist.step: check_banned_patterns() scans each physical line independently (text.splitlines()), so it misses a banned phrase split across two source lines by Python implicit string concatenation -- a style already used throughout backend/app/api/schemas.py's own IndicatorsOut field descriptions (ATR, ADX, +DI/-DI, channel_upper/channel_lower, RSI all wrap this way), just not (currently) ProfitTargetOut's own fields. Verified directly: a description=("...today's "\n    "Autoenvelope/channel height...") input produces zero violations from check_banned_patterns(). This only matters for a brand-new file outside the 8-file known-locations list (the known 8 are independently protected by the positive per-file check regardless of line-wrapping, verified directly) -- worth having the negative check join adjacent lines (or scan the whole file text with re.DOTALL/single-string search) before matching, so its own docstring's 'anywhere in the repo, including a brand-new file' claim actually holds.

_WEEKLY_RE = re.compile(r'\bweek(ly)?\b') doesn't match the plural 'weeks' on its own (\b right after the non-'ly' branch fails since 'weeks' has no boundary between 'week' and the following 's') -- verified directly: _WEEKLY_RE.search('100 weeks') is None while _WEEKLY_RE.search('100 weekly') matches. Currently harmless since every real occurrence in the repo pairs 'weeks' with 'weekly' nearby, but a future, fully-correct edit phrasing the warm-up window as e.g. '~100 weeks of price history' without the adjective 'weekly' anywhere nearby would be wrongly flagged as a stale-daily-channel regression by check_known_files_mention_weekly. Fix the regex to r'\bweeks?(ly)?\b' (or equivalent) so the plural noun form is recognized on its own.

_iter_scanned_files() calls REPO_ROOT.rglob('*') over the entire repo tree and only filters out node_modules/.venv/.git/dist/build/coverage/etc. after full enumeration, rather than pruning those directories during traversal (e.g. an os.walk with dirnames[:] = [d for d in dirnames if d not in _EXCLUDED_DIR_NAMES]). Since this script now runs as static-verify's own step 5 -- which pr-reviewer and task-qa-reviewer both run unconditionally on every task -- this wasted walk over tens of thousands of node_modules/.venv/.git files repeats on every PR review and QA pass and will only get slower as those directories grow.

_PROFIT_TARGET_CONTEXT_RE's `profit[\s_]target` alternative doesn't match the hyphenated form 'profit-target' -- the literal text of methodologyContent.ts's own start_anchor (id: 'profit-target'). Verified directly: the id text alone doesn't match. In practice the check currently still passes because the same entry's `name` field ('Profit Target (+ reward:risk ratio)') independently matches the space-separated form -- a genuine structural field of the entry, not throwaway incidental prose, so the practical fragility is lower than it first appears, but it's still an unnecessary gap: add a hyphenated alternative (`profit[\s_-]target`) so the anchor's own id text is self-sufficient context, not reliant on a second field happening to also mention it.

_extract_region() silently falls back to scanning to the end of the file when end_anchor fails to match, with no violation/warning emitted -- asymmetric with the explicit 'this guard's start anchor no longer matches -- update...' violation raised when start_anchor fails. If a known file's structure changes so the end anchor stops matching (e.g. profitTargetHelp becomes the last export in a metricHelpContent.ts, or profit-target becomes the last id: entry in methodologyContent.ts), the scanned region would silently balloon to include unrelated trailing content (e.g. the genuinely-different DAILY trade-grading description) with no signal to a maintainer that the anchor needs updating -- worth emitting the same kind of 'anchor no longer scoping correctly, update this guard' violation in that case too, for symmetry with the start-anchor check.

scripts/check_profit_target_wording.py has one ruff finding (SIM103: `_should_scan_for_banned_patterns` could return `not _is_test_file(path)` directly instead of the trailing if/return). Not part of the enforced backend `ruff check app/` gate (scripts/ at the repo root is out of scope, same precedent as scripts/validate_tasks.py) so non-blocking, but scripts/validate_tasks.py itself -- the sibling script this one explicitly mirrors -- is fully ruff-clean, so this is a small, easy inconsistency worth tidying up to match.

decisions.decision: Fixed check_banned_patterns()'s cross-line-concatenation blind spot by recognizing Python's own implicit-string-concatenation syntax specifically (a regex matching `quote, whitespace spanning a newline, matching quote` and dropping just the quote pair, preserving every newline) rather than switching to a whole-file re.DOTALL scan or blanket whitespace-collapsing normalization.
decisions.rationale: A whole-file re.DOTALL/single-string search (the alternative floated in the checklist item itself) would also match a banned phrase split across two genuinely unrelated lines/paragraphs that just happen to have the right words in the right order with nothing else between -- a broader match surface than the bug class this guard exists for, and it would make every violation's line-number reporting harder (a match spanning many lines has no single obvious 'the' line to report). Targeting the specific implicit-concatenation syntax keeps the fix narrow to the actual reported gap (schemas.py's own Field description wrapping style) while leaving every other newline in a file inert to the banned-pattern regexes, exactly as before. It also preserves exact line-number reporting for free, since only quote characters are removed, not newlines -- a plain `joined_text.count("\n", 0, match.start())` still maps correctly back to the original file's physical lines.

decisions.decision: On a failed end_anchor (checklist item 5), emit a violation but still fall back to scanning from the start anchor to end of file, rather than skipping the file's positive check entirely the way a failed start_anchor does.
decisions.rationale: A failed start_anchor means there is no valid region at all to scan, so skipping is the only option. A failed end_anchor still leaves a well-defined region start; the fallback-to-end-of-file region is a superset that still legitimately contains the real profit-target description (just with extra, possibly-unrelated trailing content risked), so scanning it can still catch a real regression even while the guard's own anchor needs a maintainer's attention -- silently disabling the positive check entirely on a stale end_anchor would be a worse outcome than an occasional extra false positive from bleeding into trailing content.

decisions.decision: Refactored _iter_scanned_files() to os.walk with dirnames[:] pruning (checklist item 3) but left the now-redundant _EXCLUDED_DIR_NAMES membership check inside _should_scan_for_banned_patterns() in place, as a defense-in-depth safety net for any future caller of that predicate outside the pruned os.walk loop, with a comment noting the redundancy.
decisions.rationale: Removing it would save a negligible amount of work per call and add a hidden coupling: _should_scan_for_banned_patterns() would only be a correct 'should this file be scanned' predicate when called from inside _iter_scanned_files()'s own pruned walk, silently wrong if called on an arbitrary path from anywhere else. Verified the traversal refactor is fully behavior-preserving by diffing the real repo's scanned-file set (217 files, byte-for-byte identical sorted path list) between the pre-change rglob-based implementation and the new os.walk-based one.

decisions.decision: Fixed PR #226's needs_work finding (the implicit-concatenation join false-flagging unrelated quoted prose/code) by (a) restricting `_join_implicit_string_concatenation` to `.py` files only in `check_banned_patterns`, and (b) rewriting the join itself to use the stdlib `tokenize` module instead of a bare regex: it now walks the real token stream and only merges two `STRING` tokens that are adjacent with nothing but `COMMENT`/`NL`/indentation tokens between them. This is the correct scoping because Python's grammar only allows two string literals to be adjacent tokens across a physical line break (as opposed to two separate statements) when they sit inside an open bracket or a backslash continuation -- outside of one, the tokenizer emits a logical-line-ending `NEWLINE` token between them instead of the non-logical `NL` used inside brackets, and a `NEWLINE` now always breaks the join.
decisions.rationale: Rejected two narrower regex patches: (1) just adding a same-quote-character check with a bracket-depth counter re-implemented by hand -- this duplicates exactly what CPython's own tokenizer already gets right (string prefixes, escaped quotes, triple-quotes, nested brackets inside strings) and risks its own new edge-case bugs; `tokenize` is stdlib (no new dependency, consistent with this script's stdlib-only philosophy) and is definitionally correct for 'is this genuine Python implicit string concatenation'. (2) Restricting to `.py` files alone without the tokenize rewrite -- this would still have false-flagged the reviewer's second repro (two unrelated bare string-literal statements in a `.py` file), since the old regex only checked for matching quote characters, not real token adjacency. Verified directly: reproduced both of the reviewer's false-positive repros (the .md two-unrelated-sentences case and the .py two-unrelated-bare-statements case) against the pre-fix code, confirmed both are now silent (no violations) against the post-fix code, and confirmed the original checklist item 1 case (schemas.py's own Field description implicit-concatenation wrapping style) is still correctly flagged. Added two new regression tests (`test_unrelated_quoted_sentences_across_a_line_break_in_md_are_not_flagged`, `test_unrelated_bare_string_statements_in_py_are_not_flagged`) alongside the pre-existing real-implicit-concatenation regression test so all three stay pinned going forward.

decisions.decision: Fixed PR #226's round-3 blocking findings by replacing the whole-file 'joined text' buffer approach entirely: `check_banned_patterns` now (a) scans each physical line of the untouched original text independently for `_BANNED_PATTERNS` (never crossing a real newline, so it can no longer bridge an ordinary unrelated line break in any file type), and (b) separately finds every genuine implicit-string-concatenation run via a new `_iter_implicit_concat_runs` (same tokenize-based adjacency logic as before, but now just identifying token runs instead of mutating a text buffer), decodes each run's *real* string values with `ast.literal_eval` (what Python's own runtime would actually produce -- no injected whitespace, no leftover newline), concatenates just those decoded values, and matches `_BANNED_PATTERNS` against that small per-run string. A match's line number is now always either the real physical line of the per-line scan, or the real tokenize-reported start line of whichever token in the run the match falls in -- never derived from a shared, edited buffer.
decisions.rationale: Rejected keeping the single shared 'joined' buffer and trying to patch its `\s+`-crosses-any-newline problem with a mask of 'safe to bridge' offsets -- tracking which newlines are join-legitimate versus ordinary inside one big regex-scanned string, while also keeping post-replacement offsets mapped back to pre-replacement line numbers, is exactly the kind of fragile, easy-to-get-subtly-wrong bookkeeping that produced both round-3 bugs in the first place (one whole-text `\s+` match spanning an unrelated newline, one line-number-desyncing replacement span). Scoping each run's scan to its own small, independently-decoded value sidesteps both classes of bug at once: the per-line scan physically cannot span a newline (no buffer edits, no cross-line regex), and a run's own line-number reporting comes straight from tokenize's real `(row, col)` positions, so no join earlier in a file can ever perturb a violation's reported location later in the file. Verified directly: reproduced all three of round 3's exact false-positive repros (.md, .ts, .py-with-an-ordinary-docstring) against the pre-fix code and confirmed all three are silent post-fix; reproduced the reviewer's 7-line line-number-desync repro (a join on lines 3-4, a real violation on line 7) and confirmed the violation is now reported at line 7, not 6; reconfirmed the original checklist item 1 case (schemas.py-style Field description split across two implicitly-concatenated literals) is still caught; reconfirmed both round-2 false-positive repros (unrelated quoted sentences in .md, unrelated bare string statements in .py) are still silent. Added four new regression tests covering all of the above plus the existing 26; full suite (30 tests) plus the pre-existing `test_validate_tasks.py` suite (52 total) pass, ruff and mypy are clean on both changed files, and the real guard run against the repo tree stays clean (217 files scanned, 0 violations).

decisions.decision: Fixed PR #226's round-4 blocking findings (both in `_find_run_violations`) by (a) reporting the real source line a match's text starts on -- `token.start[0]` plus a count of the token's own decoded newlines up to the match's offset within it -- instead of the token's opening line, correctly handling a match that starts partway into a multi-line token (e.g. a triple-quoted string implicitly concatenated to another literal); and (b) only reporting a run-based match at all when it genuinely crosses from one member literal's decoded span into another's (`_span_index_for_offset(match.start()) != _span_index_for_offset(match.end() - 1)`) -- a match sitting entirely within a single member literal is now silently skipped there, left to the ordinary per-line scan (or, if the phrase is split only by a literal newline inside one un-concatenated multi-line token, to the already-tracked, deliberately-accepted gap noted in round 4's own non-blocking finding #4).
decisions.rationale: Rejected re-introducing any form of whole-run offset-to-line lookup table (e.g. precomputing every newline position across the full run up front) as unnecessary complexity: because a member literal's decoded value's own embedded newlines correspond 1:1 to that literal's real source line breaks for the plain-string case this guard's banned patterns actually appear in (prose in triple-quoted docstrings/Field descriptions, not string literals built from escaped `\n` sequences), counting newlines within just the one piece the match starts in is sufficient and keeps the fix local to `_find_run_violations`, matching round 3's own precedent of preferring narrow, per-function fixes over larger structural rewrites once the run-decoding approach itself was already correct. For the second bug, rejected deduplicating by cross-referencing the per-line scan's own reported line numbers (e.g. suppressing a run-based hit if that same line already got a per-line hit) -- that would still leave the run-based scan actively mislabeling a same-line, non-split match as 'split across an implicit string concatenation' in the case where the per-line and run-based scans happened to run in the other order or matched different pattern instances, whereas checking whether the match structurally crosses a piece boundary is a direct, order-independent test of the actual claim the label makes. Considered whether either fix could introduce a round-5 regression: the boundary-crossing check uses `end() - 1` (not `end()`) so a match ending exactly at a piece's upper edge is correctly attributed to that piece rather than spuriously treated as crossing into a nonexistent next piece; the newline-counting fix only changes which line is reported, never whether a match is found, so it can't introduce a new false negative, and it doesn't touch the already-correct single-line-token case (0 newlines before the match still yields the token's own start line, unchanged from before). Reconstructed both of round 4's exact repro scenarios from scratch (a triple-quoted string spanning source lines 2-3 implicitly concatenated to a second literal on line 4, with the banned phrase split across the string boundary starting on line 3 -- now correctly reported at line 3, not line 2; and a banned phrase sitting entirely within one member literal on line 2 of a two-literal run -- now reported exactly once, by the per-line scan, with no second mislabeled run-based hit) as new regression tests, plus reconfirmed every pre-existing regression test (all three round-2/3 false-positive scenarios, the original schemas.py-style genuine-split case, the round-3 line-number-desync case, and the round-4 fix report's own join-at-mid-word/three-way-join cases implicit in the existing suite) still passes. Full scripts/tests suite (32 tests, up from 30) plus test_validate_tasks.py (54 total) pass; ruff is clean on the diff (the one pre-existing SIM110 finding on `_is_excluded_path`, already tracked in this task's own checklist item 6 and in the not-yet-worked `-followups-followups-followups` task, is untouched by this change); mypy is clean; the real guard run against the live repo tree stays clean (217 files scanned, 0 violations).

decisions.decision: Treated this round-4 fix as answering the parked `questions` entry's option (a) ("authorize one more fix round targeting exactly these two findings") rather than raising a new question or leaving the task at `waiting_input` -- the dispatch that started this session explicitly named both round-4 findings and instructed fixing them directly, which is the human-in-the-loop decision the parked question was waiting on. The `questions` entry itself is left untouched (append-only historical record, per CLAUDE.md's decision-memory convention) rather than edited or removed.
decisions.rationale: CLAUDE.md's `questions`/`waiting_input` convention exists so a worker doesn't keep guessing at a call only a human can make -- once a human (here, via the orchestrating dispatch) has actually made that call, the right move is to resume the task and record that the question was answered, not to re-raise the same question or treat the retry-cap parking as still in effect. No alternative was considered: the dispatch instructions were unambiguous about which option was chosen and exactly what to fix, so this was a record of an already-made decision, not a judgment call task-worker made on its own.

decisions.decision: Fixed both of PR #226's round-5 blocking findings (the escaped-newline wrong-line-number bug, and the addendum missed-detection bug) with one structural rewrite of `_find_run_violations`'s line-attribution and boundary-crossing logic, rather than another narrow patch, per the round-5 dispatch's explicit instruction that this was the third attempt at this exact function's line-number logic. Replaced `ast.literal_eval`-only decoding with a new hand-written, offset-tracking string-literal decoder (`_decode_body_with_offsets`/`_decode_string_token_with_offsets`) that walks each STRING token's own raw source text (prefix/quote/body, escape table per the language reference) while recording, for every decoded character produced, the exact raw offset within the token's own untouched source text (`tok.string`) it came from. A reported line number is now always computed by mapping a match's offset in the decoded value back to that raw offset (`_physical_line_for_offset`), then counting real `\n` bytes in the untouched raw text up to that point -- never by counting `\n` characters in re-decoded text, which is what caused round 5's escaped-newline bug (an escape-produced decoded newline character has no corresponding real source line break). Separately, replaced the boundary-crossing guard's condition from "does the match cross a piece index" to "does the match cross a piece index OR a real physical line within one piece" (comparing `_physical_line_for_offset` at `match.start()` vs. `match.end() - 1`, now that both are anchored in real coordinates) -- this directly fixes the addendum false negative, since a match sitting entirely within one multi-line piece (split only by that piece's own real embedded newline) now correctly fails the "same physical line" half of the skip condition and gets reported, whereas before it only checked piece identity and wrongly skipped it. As a safety net given this is a hand-rolled decoder (not a stdlib call), `_decode_string_token_with_offsets` cross-checks its own decoded value against `ast.literal_eval`'s (real ground truth) and returns `None` (causing the whole run to be safely skipped, matching the pre-existing behavior for f-strings/byte-strings) on any mismatch -- so a gap in this decoder's own escape-sequence coverage can only ever result in a skip, never a wrong line number silently reported.
decisions.rationale:
Rejected patching the existing decoded-newline-counting approach a third time (e.g. special-casing 'subtract escape-produced newlines from the count') -- that's exactly the kind of narrow, reactive patch the dispatch explicitly asked not to repeat, and it doesn't fix the addendum's missed-detection bug at all, which lives in the separate boundary-crossing condition, not the line-counting one. Rejected reimplementing line attribution by counting newlines in the *raw* token substring the match nominally corresponds to without a real offset map (e.g. approximating via `len(raw prefix) / len(decoded prefix)` ratios) -- that's exactly the kind of heuristic the dispatch called out as unsound; only a real per-character offset map, built by walking the token's own escape grammar the same way CPython's own parser does, is anchored in true tokenizer coordinates end to end. Considered reimplementing decoding via a lower-level use of the `tokenize`/`ast` modules (e.g. `ast.parse` node `col_offset`s) instead of a hand-written escape-table decoder, but `ast` only gives token-level (not per-character) source positions -- the same granularity `tokenize` already provides -- so there is no stdlib call that maps an arbitrary decoded-string offset back to a raw source offset; a hand-rolled decoder following the language reference's own documented, finite escape-sequence grammar was the smallest correct primitive, and the `ast.literal_eval` cross-check closes the residual risk of hand-rolling it slightly wrong (verified this safety net actually engages: found and fixed one real decoder bug this way during development -- an initial octal-escape implementation incorrectly masked the decoded codepoint to `& 0xFF` [correct for bytes literals, wrong for str literals per direct `ast.literal_eval` verification: `\501` decodes to `chr(0o501)` = 'Ł', not `chr(0o501 & 0xFF)` = 'A'] -- caught by comparing against `ast.literal_eval` during manual verification before this was ever exercised through the guard's real matching path). Verified both round-5 repros directly: the escaped-newline case (a single-physical-line piece containing a literal `
` escape, phrase crossing into the next run piece) now reports line 2, not line 3; the addendum case (`"""today's
    Autoenvelope"""` implicitly concatenated to `"trailing"`) now reports a violation at line 2 instead of silently returning zero violations. Also verified all of round 3's and round 4's own repros still pass unchanged (all 54 pre-existing scripts/tests), and added 5 new regression tests: the two exact round-5 repros, plus three further escape-sequence edge cases (a `	` escape before the match, a raw string's literal `
` two-character escape, and multiple different escape sequences in one piece) to build confidence this isn't yet another narrowly-scoped fix -- none of the five surfaced a further bug. Additionally spot-verified the hand-rolled decoder against `\x`, `\u`, `\U`, `\N{...}`, octal, an unrecognized escape, a backslash-newline line continuation, and raw/byte/f-string prefix skipping, comparing every case's output directly against `ast.literal_eval` (all matched after the octal fix above; byte-strings and f-strings correctly return `None`/skip, as before). Full suite results: `scripts/tests` 59/59 (up from 54); real guard run against the live repo tree clean (258 files, 0 violations); backend `pytest --cov=app --cov-fail-under=90` 1239 passed, 100% coverage; frontend `vitest --coverage` 91 files / 879 tests passed, 99.7%+ across all four metrics; backend ruff and mypy clean on both changed files (mypy run directly against `scripts/check_profit_target_wording.py`, which is outside its enforced `files = ["app"]` scope but has been kept clean every round per this task's own precedent); frontend eslint and tsc clean (unrelated to this change, run as a final sanity sweep). Noted but deliberately left out of scope: a pre-existing, unrelated potential gap in the *plain per-line scan* (not `_find_run_violations`) where an escaped quote character inside a single, non-run string literal could break a raw-text regex match even though the decoded value would match -- this affects any single string literal (not specific to runs) and predates every round of this review lineage, so it's not a regression introduced by this fix and not part of the round-5 dispatch's mandate (this function's line-number/boundary logic specifically); left unfixed and unfiled rather than expanding scope further on the third attempt at this exact function.

decisions.decision: Fixed all three of PR #226's round-6 blocking findings in `_iter_implicit_concat_runs` with one combined rewrite: (1) removed the different-physical-line requirement from the adjacency check entirely, and (2) removed the matching-quote-character requirement entirely, replacing both with a single, provably-sufficient condition -- rewrote the function to walk the token stream with an explicit index (instead of a plain `for tok in tokens` loop) so that reaching a candidate member (a STRING token, or an f-string -- see below) with the previous candidate still on record is now, by construction, the *only* thing the adjacency check relies on: `_NON_BREAKING_TOKEN_TYPES` are the sole token types ever skipped without resetting that record, so anything else in between (crucially a real `tokenize.NEWLINE`) has already cleared it before a new candidate is reached. This drops both spurious extra conditions (same-line-forbidden, matching-quote-required) without weakening genuine-implicit-concatenation detection at all, since Python's own grammar never required either of them -- they were both carryovers from the original regex-based join. (3) For f-strings (PEP 701's FSTRING_START/MIDDLE/END on this project's Python 3.12): chose option (b) from the two offered in this round's dispatch -- recognize the whole FSTRING_START..FSTRING_END span as one opaque run member (a new `_find_fstring_end_index` walks forward tracking nesting depth to find the real matching FSTRING_END, including for a nested f-string), using the FSTRING_START token itself (`.end` extended to the f-string's true end) as the run member's stand-in. This correctly participates in adjacency (a plain string immediately before or after a run-forming f-string is recognized as genuinely part of the same run, rather than the f-string's presence silently resetting the whole chain to invisible) but is never decoded -- `_decode_string_token_with_offsets` already, unconditionally, returns `None` for anything with an `f` in its raw prefix (verified this is hit regardless of how `_parse_string_literal` happens to (mis)parse an FSTRING_START token's own incomplete `.string`, e.g. `f"` or `f"""`, since the `f`-in-prefix check runs before any use of the parsed body) -- which safely skips the *entire* run it's a member of via `_find_run_violations`'s own pre-existing any-member-undecodable-skips-the-whole-run contract, identical to how a byte-string run is already handled.
decisions.rationale: Rejected option (a) (fully extracting and decoding an f-string's own literal-only content, joining multiple FSTRING_MIDDLE pieces where present) as disproportionate engineering effort with a real new-bug surface for a guard that has already needed correction across three separate axes over 6 review rounds (line-number arithmetic in rounds 3-5, run-detection-itself in round 6): an f-string's *general* value genuinely isn't statically knowable at all once it contains any `{expr}` interpolation (the common case -- the whole reason to reach for an f-string in real code), so full (a) could only ever handle a narrower special case (interpolation-free f-strings) while still needing all the new machinery (joining multiple MIDDLE tokens, handling PEP 701's own doubled-brace unescaping already partially applied at the tokenizer level, distinguishing a genuinely-empty MIDDLE from an absent one) -- exactly the kind of narrow-but-intricate string-literal-grammar code that produced rounds 3-5's escalating bugs in the first place, for a benefit (catching a banned phrase specifically split across an f-string boundary) this guard's own description/decisions already establish is secondary: `check_known_files_mention_weekly`'s per-file positive check independently and unconditionally catches a reversion in any of the 8 known regression-prone files regardless of this repo-wide negative check's precision. Verified the chosen design directly against the exact edge case this round's dispatch called out for careful reasoning -- an f-string sitting between two real string literals in what would otherwise be one run (`"today's " f"middle {1}" "Autoenvelope"`): confirmed it does NOT incorrectly bridge the two real strings across the f-string as if it weren't there (which would risk a false positive from treating unrelated, real f-string content as if absent) -- the whole 3-member run is recognized as such, then safely skipped in its entirety once the f-string member's decode returns `None`, never partially or incorrectly evaluated. Also directly reproduced and confirmed the fix for round 6's own three repro scenarios (same-line concatenation, mixed quote-style concatenation, and the f-string-run recognition case -- the latter remains a documented, deliberate non-detection per the (b) choice above, not a crash or a new false positive) and reconfirmed every prior round's existing regression test (all 59 pre-change tests) still passes unchanged. Added 4 new regression tests (same-line concat, mixed-quote concat, f-string-run-safely-skipped, f-string-between-two-real-strings-does-not-bridge) reconstructed from scratch per this round's dispatch instructions. Full suite results: scripts/tests 63/63 (up from 59); real guard run against the live repo tree clean (258 files scanned, 0 violations); scripts/validate_tasks.py clean; backend ruff/mypy clean (mypy run directly against scripts/check_profit_target_wording.py, outside its enforced files=["app"] scope but kept clean every round per this task's own precedent) and pytest --cov=app --cov-fail-under=90: 1239 passed, 100% coverage; frontend vitest --coverage: 91 files / 879 tests passed, 99.7%+ across all four metrics (untouched by this change, run as a final sanity sweep).

questions.question: PR #226 has now hit 3 consecutive needs_work rounds, each fixing the previous round's finding but introducing a new bug in the same implicit-string-concatenation handling in scripts/check_profit_target_wording.py. Round 4's outstanding findings are two more edge-case bugs in the same area (a multi-line-token run reports the wrong line number; a phrase sitting entirely within one member literal of a run gets double-reported with a misleading label). Per the orchestrator's 3-round retry cap, this is being parked rather than retried a 4th time. How do you want to proceed: (a) authorize one more fix round targeting exactly these two findings, (b) accept the current behavior as good enough (both are narrow edge cases -- a multi-line string inside an implicit-concat run, and a non-split phrase within a run -- neither is present anywhere in the current repo, and neither causes a missed detection, only a wrong/duplicate report) and merge as-is with the two findings tracked as known-accepted follow-ups instead of blockers, or (c) simplify the guard script's scope (e.g. drop the implicit-concatenation run-matching feature entirely, keeping only the per-line scan plus the per-file positive check that already independently protects the 8 known regression-prone files) to stop the escalating edge-case chase. comments.summary: BLOCKING (round 6): `_iter_implicit_concat_runs` requires the two adjacent STRING tokens to be on *different* physical lines (`prev_string_token.end[0] != tok.start[0]`) to treat them as a run -- silently assuming a same-line split is already caught by the per-line scan. That assumption is false: the raw text between the two literals on one line still has the closing-quote/space/opening-quote characters of the join interposed between the split words, which the banned-pattern regexes' `\s+` can't bridge. Verified directly: `description = "Current price + 30% of today's " "Autoenvelope/channel height."` (all one physical line) evaluates at runtime to the exact banned phrase, but `check_banned_patterns` returns `[]` -- a true false negative, independently confirmed by a backgrounded `code-review` (effort high) pass against this same diff.

BLOCKING (round 6): `_iter_implicit_concat_runs` additionally requires the raw closing-quote character of the first STRING token to equal the raw opening-quote character of the second (`prev_string_token.string[-1:] == tok.string[:1]`) -- but Python's grammar has no such requirement; `"a" 'b'`, `'a' "b"`, and `"""a""" 'b'` are all ordinary, valid implicit concatenation. Traced this condition's origin: it's a direct carryover from the *original regex-based* join (`_STRING_CONCAT_JOIN_RE = (["'])(\s*
\s*)\1`, a backreference requiring the same quote char -- a known, accepted gap of that old regex approach, tracked as checklist item 2 on backend-profit-target-weekly-channel-followups-followups-followups). When the join was rewritten to use real tokenize-based type checking, this heuristic should have been dropped as redundant (since `tok.type == tokenize.STRING` plus the surrounding NL/COMMENT-only adjacency check is already fully sufficient proof of genuine concatenation), but it was carried over unnoticed. Verified directly: `description = (
    "Current price + 30% of today's "
    'Autoenvelope/channel height.'
)` evaluates to the exact banned phrase; `check_banned_patterns` returns `[]`. Independently confirmed by the same backgrounded `code-review` pass.

BLOCKING (round 6): `_iter_implicit_concat_runs` only treats `tok.type == tokenize.STRING` as a candidate run member. On Python 3.12 (this project's own required version), an f-string tokenizes via PEP 701 into `FSTRING_START`/`FSTRING_MIDDLE`/`FSTRING_END` tokens, not `tokenize.STRING` -- none of which are in `_NON_BREAKING_TOKEN_TYPES`, so any one of them resets `current_run`/`prev_string_token` entirely. This means a real implicit-concatenation run involving an f-string piece is never even considered a run -- not the graceful, `ast.literal_eval`-cross-checked skip that `_decode_string_token_with_offsets`'s own `"f" in prefix_lower: return None` implies was intended (that code is unreachable for a pure f-string on this Python version, since the token never reaches it). Verified directly: `description = (
    f"Current price + 30% of today's "
    "Autoenvelope/channel height."
)` evaluates to the exact banned phrase at runtime; `check_banned_patterns` returns `[]`. Independently confirmed by the same backgrounded `code-review` pass, which additionally confirmed via a direct `tokenize.generate_tokens` dump on Python 3.12.14 that the FSTRING_* token sequence (not a single STRING token) is what actually breaks the chain.

Also stress-tested the hand-rolled decoder (`_decode_body_with_offsets`/`_decode_string_token_with_offsets`) against `\x`, `\u`, `\U`, `\N{...}`, unrecognized escapes, backslash-newline continuation, raw strings, and nested/escaped-quote forms, all matching `ast.literal_eval` exactly, and specifically tried to construct a case where the decoded *value* would match ground truth while the *offset* attribution was wrong (the one gap the cross-check can't itself catch) -- could not construct one; the offset bookkeeping is sound by inspection for every escape form in the documented grammar. Byte-string-only runs (`b"..." b"..."`) have the same structural cross-line-miss gap as f-strings (same root cause: `_decode_string_token_with_offsets` returns `None` for the whole run), not filed separately since bytes literals holding this kind of descriptive prose is not a realistic pattern in this codebase.
